Science.title: Molecular pendulum shuttles protons to enable rapid hydrogen production in enzymes

Enzymes from microorganisms can produce hydrogen (H₂) by combining electrons with protons. These so-called hydrogenases are so efficient that one biocatalyst can capture nearly 10,000 protons per second.

Science.title: New wheat disease detection tool established in Tanzania
Science.summary: John Innes Centre researchers have trained scientists from across Tanzania to use new loop-mediated isothermal amplification (LAMP) assays to rapidly detect wheat blast, a looming fungal threat to wheat harvests.

Science.title: A simple touch can bring dying corals back to life in just 7 weeks
Science.summary: Scientists have discovered that severely bleached corals can make a remarkable comeback simply by touching healthy, genetically identical corals. In laboratory experiments, dying corals regained their color and fully recovered within seven weeks, with as little as five days of contact sometimes enough to start the healing process.

Science.title: Planetary 'twins' Uranus and Neptune may have different origin stories
Science.summary: By indirectly probing the depths of Uranus and Neptune's atmospheres, an international team of scientists has revealed a significant contrast in their chemical composition. Neptune appears to be more enriched in oxygen than Uranus. These results suggest that the two ice giants may have formed in different regions of the primitive solar system before reaching their current orbits, calling into question the idea of a common origin for these two planets, often considered twins.

Science.title: Forgotten particle could answer mystery of why we exist, say physicists
Science.summary: Scientists have unveiled a new theory on the birth of the cosmos, suggesting the early universe was shaped by an ancient particle that has been overlooked for decades.

Science.title: Students take up to 88 standardized tests before high school, but more testing doesn't improve learning
Science.summary: The public K-12 school system in the United States has become pervasively shaped by standardized testing.

Science.title: Toxic chemicals in fentanyl revealed by speedy technique
Science.summary: Nature, Published online: 19 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03317-3 Chemical fingerprinting charts the rises and declines of specific adulterants in illicit supplies of the drug.

Science.title: The X-Files Lego set is a wonderful bit of 90s sci-fi nostalgia
Science.summary: Brick by brick ... the truth is out there. You can now own a little piece of that with this 1,478-piece Lego set

Science.title: Modern neuroscience is rediscovering a surprising idea freud had 130 years ago
Science.summary: Researchers have identified striking parallels between Sigmund Freud’s century-old theories and modern neuroscience, suggesting that the brain’s constant predictions shape how we experience reality. The findings could help explain why harmful thought patterns are so difficult to break and offer new insights into treating mental disorders.

Science.title: Criminal justice researchers use statistical modeling to examine wrongful-conviction risk
Science.summary: A University of Mississippi study is adding nuance to a debate over how often police interrogation tactics can produce false confessions leading to wrongful convictions. In a recent simulation study published in the Journal of Criminal Justice, Ole Miss criminal justice and legal studies professors Mary Catlin and Thomas Bryan Smith found that the predicted likelihood of a false confession grows with the length of a police interrogation.

Science.title: New 4D biofabrication technology holds promise for tissue engineering, wound healing
Science.summary: If you've ever created a snowflake by folding, cutting and unfolding a piece of paper, you've practiced the art of kirigami. Like origami, kirigami has inspired innovations far beyond the elementary school classroom, with applications ranging from deployable structures for spacecraft to semiconductors.

Science.title: Light and mirrors move large quantum computers closer to reality
Science.summary: Nature, Published online: 19 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03237-2 Scientists improve photon-collecting device that could be used to connect multiple quantum-computing arrays.

Science.title: Experienced researchers ‘disrupt’ less than rookie scientists — but their ideas last
Science.summary: Nature, Published online: 19 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03339-x Researchers have found a link between a scientist’s experience and and whether their ideas have a lasting influence.

Science.title: Why failure is a taboo topic in science
Science.summary: Nature, Published online: 19 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03328-0 Failure is one of the best teachers we have. So why is nobody talking about it?

Science.title: Lessons from Katrina: how to rebuild academia from the ground up
Science.summary: Nature, Published online: 19 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-02623-0 More than 20 years after Hurricane Katrina, universities in New Orleans have learnt what it takes to rebuild from ruin — including what gets in the way.

Science.title: Audio long read: How to stay smart in the age of AI — the science of critical thinking
Science.summary: Nature, Published online: 19 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03228-3 Although worries are growing about AI's potential to blunt reasoning skills, research has uncovered ways to keep the brain sharp.

Science.title: Researchers unlock new way to map molecular structure on surfaces
Science.summary: Scientists at NPL, with the University of Surrey, University of Oxford, the Francis Crick Institute and IONTOF GmbH, have developed a technique to distinguish and map molecules that share the same chemical formula and mass but have different structures and functions. The research is published today (Oct. 19) in Nature Communications.

Science.title: 'They're kind of goth': NASA spacecraft gives mysterious brown dwarfs a close-up
Science.summary: Using NASA’s SPHEREx spacecraft, astronomers have studied a horde of mysterious "failed stars," or brown dwarfs, not-so-stellar loners that wander the darkness of space alone.

Science.title: Synthetic molecules self-assemble into triple helices with new control method
Science.summary: Researchers at the University of Jyväskylä, Finland, have developed a new strategy for programming synthetic molecules to self-assemble into precisely defined three-dimensional structures. The study brings scientists a step closer to achieving the sophisticated molecular organization found in nature and could eventually open new possibilities for the development of advanced functional materials.

Science.title: Who speaks for Mars? Scientists call for ethical debate before terraforming begins
Science.summary: Transforming Mars into a more Earth-like world could irreversibly destroy scientific evidence about the planet's history and the possibility of extraterrestrial life. In an opinion article published in Eos, a team of Dutch, French and U.S. planetary scientists and ethicists warns that humanity risks destroying Mars' scientific record before it has been fully explored.

Science.title: Why the Drake equation is still important 65 years after its creation
Science.summary: The Drake equation provides a way to guess how many aliens we might be able to communicate with, but it’s also a prime example of the importance of scientific guessing, says columnist Leah Crane

Science.title: Scientists are growing human brain tissue in living mice—could this make their welfare harder to assess?
Science.summary: What happens when scientists start changing the brain—the very system through which an animal's mental states are expressed in behavior?

Science.title: Did a giant object collide with Earth to form the moon?
Science.summary: Known as the giant-impact hypothesis, this proposed event involves a collision between Earth and a hypothetical Mars-sized protoplanet astronomers call Theia.

Science.title: How to compare and strengthen research systems
Science.summary: Nature, Published online: 19 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03309-3 Analysing national research systems by using open-access data and new methods can help countries to learn from each other.
